paragraphs: The paper studies whether an autonomous agent can improve a language model’s reasoning by writing instructions for it. The agent generates one instruction set for each task, which is then used across that task’s instances. This makes the intervention a reusable guide to approaching a task, rather than a separately generated instruction set for every individual question.

The authors evaluate the method on 29 datasets covering generation, classification, and reasoning. They report that it generalizes to most of these tasks and achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot results on 20 datasets. The improvements extend across different language models, including Vicuna-13b, Llama-2-70b-chat, and GPT-3.5 Turbo, supporting the usefulness of task-level instructions across multiple model families.

The reported gains also exceed those from zero-shot chain-of-thought prompting. In one highlighted comparison, Llama-2-70b-chat using the method significantly outperforms zero-shot GPT-3.5 Turbo. These findings suggest that automatically generated reasoning guidance can substantially improve the capabilities elicited from an existing model, with the demonstrated breadth grounded in the evaluated tasks.
icml-2024-agent-instructs-large-language.tldr: An autonomous agent writes reusable task instructions that improve language models’ zero-shot performance across a broad evaluation.

paragraphs: Dataset condensation compresses a large training dataset into a small synthetic dataset for training other models. This paper asks what happens when the original data contain misleading associations. Its evaluations distinguish color, background, and corruption biases, showing that compression can affect different kinds of bias differently rather than simply preserving the original dataset’s behavior.

In the studied settings, condensation amplifies color and background biases, reducing the performance of models trained on the synthetic data. Corruption bias, however, is suppressed. To address the harmful amplification, the authors introduce a sample reweighting approach based on kernel density estimation. The method changes how samples contribute to condensation, and experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support its effectiveness.

A highlighted CMNIST result uses a 5% bias-conflict ratio and 50 images per class. The proposed method reaches 91.5% test accuracy, compared with 23.8% for vanilla DM and 53.7% for the cited debiasing method. The improvement over vanilla DM is 67.7 percentage points. This example illustrates how addressing bias during condensation can materially affect the usefulness of the resulting training data.
icml-2024-ameliorate-spurious-correlatio.tldr: Dataset condensation can amplify color and background biases, and density-based sample reweighting substantially reduces this problem in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: This paper examines how much feature learning can happen after just one gradient descent step in a two-layer neural network. The central question is how adapting a network to its data can improve on the kernel regime. Even this short training process provides a setting for studying the change from initial representations to features shaped by the learning problem.

The authors represent the trained network using a spiked random features model. They derive an exact asymptotic description of that model’s generalization error when the sample count, network width, and input dimension all grow proportionally. The proportional high-dimensional limit is central to the result: the exact characterization concerns this setting and the random features model.

The resulting predictions also closely track the learning curves of the original neural network. They reveal how data adaptation enables efficient learning of nonlinear functions along the gradient direction, where the initialized network can express only linear functions in the studied regime. This connects a precise mathematical description of generalization to a concrete explanation of what the training step changes.
icml-2024-asymptotics-of-feature-learnin.tldr: A high-dimensional analysis explains how one gradient step enables a two-layer network to learn nonlinear structure along the gradient direction.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning often estimates value by combining rewards over several future steps. Looking farther ahead can improve learning from limited experience, but it also increases variability in these estimates. This paper studies compound returns, which combine multiple n-step returns through a weighted average, as a way to reduce that variability.

The main theorem compares a compound return with an n-step return having the same contraction modulus. Under this matching condition, the compound return has strictly lower variance. The authors also prove that the reduction improves finite-sample complexity for temporal-difference learning with linear function approximation. This connects the statistical benefit of averaging to a learning guarantee in a specified approximation setting.

General compound returns can be costly to compute, so the paper introduces two-bootstrap returns as an efficient alternative that retains variance reduction, including with minibatched experience replay. Experiments with deep reinforcement learning agents such as DQN and PPO show that compound returns often improve sample efficiency. The empirical finding extends the practical motivation beyond the linear setting covered by the finite-sample result.
icml-2024-averaging-n-step-returns-reduc.tldr: Weighted averages of multistep returns reduce variance under a matched contraction condition and often improve deep reinforcement learning’s sample efficiency.

paragraphs: When a model is uncertain, presenting several possible answers can give a person more useful guidance than presenting a single prediction. Conformal prediction produces calibrated sets of possible answers, with larger sets communicating greater uncertainty. This paper tests whether that form of uncertainty communication actually helps people make more accurate decisions.

The authors conduct a pre-registered randomized controlled trial in which human participants receive prediction sets. The comparison is between conformal sets and fixed-size sets with the same coverage guarantee. Matching coverage makes the comparison particularly informative: both forms of assistance provide the same stated guarantee about including the correct answer, while differing in how the alternatives communicate uncertainty.

Participants given conformal prediction sets achieve statistically significantly higher task accuracy. The result supports using calibrated, variable-size answer sets as an aid in human-AI decision making. Its significance is that an uncertainty representation can improve the human’s eventual choice, beyond simply providing a technically meaningful guarantee about the model’s output.
icml-2024-conformal-prediction-sets-impr.tldr: A randomized trial finds that conformal prediction sets improve human accuracy compared with fixed-size sets offering the same coverage guarantee.

paragraphs: Keeping training data with individual participants does not eliminate privacy risks, because shared model updates can still expose information. This paper studies decentralized learning in which a model travels between connected participants and is updated as it goes. The route follows a random walk on the network’s communication graph.

The authors analyze this process using Pairwise Network Differential Privacy, a privacy notion tailored to decentralized algorithms. They derive closed-form expressions for privacy loss between pairs of nodes. Graph-theoretic quantities describe how the communication topology affects those expressions, making the arrangement of connections an explicit part of the privacy analysis rather than treating all participants identically.

The results indicate that random-walk algorithms tend to provide stronger privacy guarantees than gossip algorithms for nodes that are close to one another. This is a qualified comparison tied to network proximity. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world graphs and datasets supplement the theory, helping connect the mathematical characterization to decentralized learning settings.
icml-2024-differentially-private-decentr.tldr: Pairwise privacy formulas reveal how network structure shapes privacy in random-walk learning, with advantages over gossip methods for nearby nodes.

paragraphs: Robustness certificates establish that adversarial examples are absent from a specified neighborhood around an input. They therefore provide evidence about where a model’s prediction is protected against changes. This paper asks whether information released through certification can also help an attacker search for changes that do cause a model to fail.

The proposed Certification Aware Attack uses certificates to construct adversarial examples while seeking small perturbations. In the reported comparisons, it produces computationally efficient norm-minimizing adversarial examples 74% more often than comparable attacks. It also reduces the median perturbation norm by more than 10%, meaning the resulting changes are smaller under the distance measure being minimized.

The findings give certificate-aware attacks two roles. They can help assess how tight certification bounds are, and they can reveal security consequences of releasing those bounds. The paper’s conclusion is that disclosure can make attacks more effective even though certificates are intended to demonstrate robustness. This concerns how certificate information is used, rather than a claim that the certified neighborhood’s guarantee is false.
icml-2024-et-tu-certifications-robustnes.tldr: An attack that uses robustness certificates finds adversarial examples more often and with smaller median perturbations in the reported comparisons.

paragraphs: Distributed training must combine updates from multiple workers, some of which may send incorrect information through errors or malicious behavior. This paper addresses such Byzantine failures while also considering computational cost and the practical difficulty of configuring robust training. Its contributions target both the combination of worker updates and the estimation of gradients.

The authors introduce the Centered Trimmed Meta Aggregator, or CTMA. It operates as a meta-aggregator that upgrades baseline aggregation methods to the optimal performance levels studied in the paper while keeping computational demands low. This approach makes improving an existing aggregator a central design choice, connecting robustness with the efficiency needed for distributed training.

The paper also brings a double-momentum gradient estimation technique into the Byzantine setting. The authors describe advantages in simplifying tuning and reducing dependence on numerous hyperparameters. Theoretical support is developed within stochastic convex optimization, and empirical evidence supports the technique’s effectiveness. Together, the contributions address the practical usability of robust training as well as its mathematical performance.
icml-2024-fault-tolerant-ml-efficient-me.tldr: CTMA and a double-momentum gradient estimator aim to make Byzantine-robust distributed training efficient and easier to tune.

paragraphs: Causal machine learning needs guarantees about how well models perform with finite data, not just methods for fitting them. This paper develops generalization bounds for causal regression to address that need. The goal is to place a rigorous upper bound on model loss while accounting for how treatment assignment varies across the population.

The technical contribution is a new change-of-measure inequality. It allows the authors to bound loss in terms of deviations in treatment propensities, which describe the chances of receiving treatment. They also show that these deviations can be bounded empirically. This links the theoretical guarantee to a quantity that can be constrained using data.

The theory remains valid in the presence of hidden confounding and violations of positivity, two difficulties explicitly addressed by the paper. The authors demonstrate the bounds on semi-synthetic and real datasets and report tight, practically useful results. The contribution is therefore a way to quantify model loss under challenging causal conditions; the stated guarantees concern these bounds rather than an assertion that those conditions disappear.
icml-2024-generalization-bounds-for-caus.tldr: New generalization bounds quantify causal regression loss and remain valid with hidden confounding and positivity violations.

paragraphs: A tokenizer determines how text is divided into the units a language model processes. This paper argues that treating it as a fixed, inherited component can overlook consequential design choices. The authors investigate how vocabulary size, the regular expression used for pre-tokenization, and tokenizer training data affect model behavior and efficiency.

They train specialized Byte-Pair Encoding tokenizers for code and conduct ablations on code generation tasks, including HumanEval and MBPP. The experiments cover both models trained from scratch and adaptation of pretrained models. The reported effects span generation speed, effective context size, memory use, and downstream performance, showing that tokenizer design affects several aspects of the system together.

The paper provides recommendations for selecting tokenizer hyperparameters and replacing a pretrained model’s tokenizer. A highlighted finding is that specialization can yield large gains in generation speed and effective context size when fine-tuning uses more than 50 billion tokens. That training scale qualifies the stated result and makes the amount of adaptation data relevant to the decision.
icml-2024-getting-the-most-out-of-your-t.tldr: Tokenizer design materially affects code language models, with substantial speed and context gains reported after specialization using more than 50 billion fine-tuning tokens.

paragraphs: Federated prompt learning adapts pretrained vision-language models through prompts across clients with different data. Personalization helps accommodate those differences, but emphasizing it too much can weaken the model’s ability to generalize. This paper focuses on preserving transferable knowledge while still allowing prompts to reflect individual clients’ needs.

The proposed FedPGP method uses pretrained CLIP to guide a shared global prompt. It then introduces a low-rank adaptation term to personalize that prompt. A prompt-wise contrastive loss brings the knowledge guidance and personalized adaptation together. The method therefore assigns explicit roles to preserving general knowledge and adjusting to client-specific data within the same learning process.

The authors evaluate generalization from base to novel categories and domains across multiple datasets with heterogeneous data. They report that FedPGP achieves a superior balance between personalization and generalization in these experiments. The findings support the idea that retaining guidance from the pretrained model can complement local adaptation, rather than requiring the shared prompt to absorb every client difference on its own.
icml-2024-harmonizing-generalization-and.tldr: FedPGP combines CLIP-guided global prompts with low-rank personalization to balance client adaptation and generalization.

paragraphs: Completing a sparse ordinal tensor means filling missing entries in a multidimensional array whose values have an ordering. The challenge is to learn interactions across several dimensions while respecting differences between ordered values. Standard positive-versus-negative contrastive comparisons do not capture all of that structure, and candidate negative samples grow combinatorially as interactions involve more dimensions.

The proposed High-Order Contrastive Tensor Completion network, HOCTC, uses attention with query expansion to capture these higher-order interactions, including when few tokens are available. It also uses the observed ordinal entries to define finer comparative levels. This gives learning more detailed guidance than a single division between matching and nonmatching examples.

An efficient sampling scheme enforces those comparisons and supplies self-supervised learning signals. The components address both the complexity of multidimensional relationships and the ordered information contained in entries. Experiments in traffic and recommender applications show promising sparse completion results, supporting the approach as a way to adapt contrastive representation learning to this form of data.
icml-2024-high-order-contrastive-learnin.tldr: HOCTC combines higher-order attention, ordinal comparisons, and efficient sampling to learn from sparse multidimensional data.

paragraphs: Hierarchical generators organize latent variables into multiple layers that work from the top down. They commonly use Gaussian priors, but these may be too restrictive to match the generator’s posterior distribution. The resulting mismatch is called the prior hole problem. This paper studies how to learn a more expressive prior for such generators.

Energy-based priors offer one route to closing that gap and have been used as complementary models in a second training stage. However, a prior spanning multiple latent layers can have many modes. Sampling from it then becomes difficult, and ineffective sampling can undermine learning of the energy-based model itself.

The authors introduce a diffusion probabilistic scheme to reduce this sampling burden and facilitate prior learning. The approach connects greater prior expressivity with a mechanism intended to make that expressivity trainable in practice. Extensive experiments report superior performance of the diffusion-learned energy-based prior on several challenging tasks, supporting the value of addressing sampling alongside the original prior mismatch.
icml-2024-learning-latent-space-hierarch.tldr: A diffusion-based learning scheme eases sampling for expressive energy-based priors in hierarchical latent-variable generators.

paragraphs: Cooperative reinforcement learning becomes difficult as the number of agents grows. Mean field control offers a tractable approach, but its assumption of many independent, weakly interacting agents is restrictive. This paper extends the framework to systems containing many similar agents alongside a small number of more complex agents.

The resulting Major-Minor Mean Field Control framework, M3FC, comes with approximation results for finite-agent control. The authors also establish that stationary policies are sufficient for optimality and provide a dynamic programming principle. These results supply a theoretical basis for decision making in the expanded model, including a connection between the mean field formulation and finite systems.

For learning, the paper introduces M3FMARL, an algorithm operating on finite-agent systems instead of directly on the limiting system. It is shown to approximate the policy gradient of the underlying M3FC decision process. Experiments across several scenarios show strong performance compared with state-of-the-art policy-gradient multi-agent methods, supporting the framework’s practical relevance for mixed populations of agents.
icml-2024-major-minor-mean-field-multi-a.tldr: Major-Minor Mean Field Control extends scalable cooperative learning to populations with many similar agents and a few complex ones.

paragraphs: Multi-view clustering combines different views of the same data to find groups that reflect both shared structure and differences between views. Many methods depend heavily on knowing the correct number of clusters beforehand. This paper addresses the more practical situation in which that number is unknown and must be inferred during clustering.

The authors propose a graph-based algorithm that evaluates cluster assignments for different candidate cluster counts at each iteration. They formulate selection of the unknown count as a reinforcement learning process. Its reward is based on connectivity between clusters, providing a graph-derived signal for comparing possible groupings and guiding the inference process.

The method produces a final clustering without requiring a predefined cluster number as input. This matters because choosing that number is incorporated into the algorithm’s work rather than supplied as prior knowledge by the user. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate effectiveness relative to existing state-of-the-art methods, supporting the use of connectivity-guided rewards for this joint inference task.
icml-2024-multi-view-clustering-by-inter.tldr: A graph-based multi-view clustering method uses connectivity rewards to infer cluster assignments and the unknown number of clusters.

paragraphs: Physics-informed learning combines observations with physical models expressed through partial differential equations. This paper adds another source of mathematical structure: a Lie symmetry of the governing equations. The authors investigate how that symmetry can constrain a Gaussian process model, bringing information from the equation’s structure into learning from data.

They provide two ways to incorporate the symmetry. One uses virtual observations of an additional equation, the invariant surface condition, to impose a soft constraint. The other builds the symmetry explicitly into the Gaussian process kernel. These options place symmetry information either into the model’s observational constraints or directly into the structure used to define the process.

Experiments show that symmetry constraints improve Gaussian process performance on both forward and inverse problems. The approach also performs competitively with neural networks in low-data settings. The findings support symmetry as a useful complement to physical equations and observations, particularly where the model must learn with limited measured information. Both implementations make that additional structure part of the inference process.
icml-2024-physics-and-lie-symmetry-infor.tldr: Adding Lie symmetry constraints to physics-informed Gaussian processes improves reported forward and inverse results, with competitive low-data performance.

paragraphs: This position paper examines what it means to call AI an ethical agent. Drawing on political science and philosophy, the authors distinguish two competing conceptions of agency. The distinction matters because the meaning assigned to agency affects both judgments about desirable AI behavior and the way accountability is understood.

The authors call the first conception mechanistic and argue that AI research commonly assumes it without making that assumption explicit. They regard it as fundamentally limited for understanding AI’s ethical characteristics. Under the second conception, which they call volitional, AI does not qualify as an ethical agent. The argument therefore makes the choice of conceptual framework central to the ethical analysis.

The paper explores what each view implies for the kind of system that ought to be built and for achieving accountability. It ultimately argues that ethically significant AI behavior should be understood as an outcome of political processes. This shifts the proposed focus of analysis toward how AI comes to take its form and how that process bears on responsibility.
icml-2024-position-beyond-personhood-age.tldr: The authors argue that AI ethics and accountability should examine AI as an outcome of political processes rather than assume ethical agency.

paragraphs: Aligning a foundation model involves deciding which behaviors it should encourage or avoid. Human input can take the form of preferences between responses, as in reinforcement learning from human feedback, or high-level principles, as in constitutional AI. This position paper focuses on what happens when the people supplying that guidance disagree.

The authors argue that social choice is well suited to studying how diverse inputs can inform collective decisions about model behavior. The question is not simply how to collect more feedback. It is also how to combine potentially conflicting judgments into consistent information about collective preferences, or otherwise use them to make decisions.

The paper develops an agenda for applying social choice to alignment, drawing on workshop discussions. Its contribution is a proposed direction for handling disagreement rather than an experimentally validated aggregation procedure. The argument highlights that alignment methods need a way to reason about whose preferences are represented and how differing human inputs become a shared behavioral objective.
icml-2024-position-social-choice-should-.tldr: This position paper argues that social choice should guide how AI alignment combines conflicting human preferences and principles.

paragraphs: Correlation clustering groups graph nodes using positive and negative edge labels. A positive edge conflicts with the clustering when its endpoints are separated; a negative edge conflicts when they are grouped together. The objective is to minimize the total number of these disagreements, making the problem useful for unsupervised grouping from pairwise relationships.

This paper studies settings motivated by large graphs and changing data: fully dynamic algorithms, massively parallel computation, and local computation. The proposed approach improves state-of-the-art runtime complexities in all three settings. These are different computational demands on the same clustering problem, so the contribution concerns how efficiently clustering can be supported under several modes of access and execution.

The highlighted result is a fully dynamic algorithm with expected amortized constant runtime, independent of graph size. The expected and amortized qualifications are part of the guarantee; it is not stated as a fixed worst-case cost for every operation. The algorithm also essentially matches the approximation guarantee of Pivot, combining the runtime improvements with a comparable guarantee on clustering quality.
icml-2024-pruned-pivot-correlation-clust.tldr: Pruned Pivot improves correlation-clustering runtimes across dynamic, parallel, and local settings while essentially retaining Pivot’s approximation guarantee.

paragraphs: Safe reinforcement learning must estimate whether a proposed policy update will satisfy its constraints. This paper identifies a mismatch in an existing approach: advantage-based estimation uses an infinite-horizon discounted quantity, while some constraints concern a finite horizon without discounting. In those scenarios, the mismatch can cause severe estimation errors and unsafe updates.

The authors introduce Gradient-based Estimation, or GBE, using an analytic gradient derived along trajectories. It is designed specifically to estimate changes in finite-horizon, nondiscounted constraints. Theoretical and empirical analyses support its effectiveness, addressing the estimation problem that determines whether the next policy is expected to remain feasible.

The paper then builds Constrained Gradient-based Policy Optimization, CGPO, around a surrogate optimization problem using GBE. The algorithm repeatedly solves subproblems within trust regions to identify feasible optimal policies. In the reported experiments, it successfully estimates subsequent policies’ constraint functions where baseline algorithms do not, supporting efficient and feasible updates in those evaluations. The practical contribution links a better-matched constraint estimator to the policy optimization procedure that uses it.
icml-2024-safe-reinforcement-learning-us.tldr: GBE estimates finite-horizon constraint changes and enables CGPO to make efficient, feasible policy updates in the reported safe reinforcement learning experiments.

paragraphs: Generating high-resolution images directly in pixel space requires an architecture that handles growing image size efficiently. This paper introduces the Hourglass Diffusion Transformer, HDiT, whose scaling is linear in pixel count. It supports training directly on images at resolutions such as 1024 by 1024, making pixel-space generation the central architectural target.

HDiT builds on Transformers while aiming to combine their ability to scale in parameter count with the efficiency associated with convolutional U-Nets. The authors report successful training without several commonly used high-resolution techniques: multiscale architectures, latent autoencoders, and self-conditioning. This demonstrates that their architecture can support the reported training settings without depending on those additional techniques.

The evaluation reports competitive performance with existing models on ImageNet at 256 by 256 resolution. On FFHQ at 1024 by 1024, it establishes a new state of the art among diffusion models. Together, these results support the architecture’s ability to pair high-resolution pixel-space training with strong image-generation performance on the evaluated benchmarks.
icml-2024-scalable-high-resolution-pixel.tldr: HDiT enables high-resolution pixel-space diffusion with linear pixel-count scaling and strong results on ImageNet and FFHQ.

paragraphs: Dataset-level scaling laws describe how performance changes as training sets grow, but they do not distinguish the contributions of individual examples. This paper studies scaling at that finer level. The authors find that a data point’s contribution to performance shrinks predictably with dataset size according to a log-linear relationship.

Different examples have substantially different scaling exponents. Consequently, points that are valuable in small datasets need not be the ones that are relatively most useful in larger datasets. The authors provide learning-theoretic support and observe the behavior across several model classes, suggesting that data value should be considered in relation to the size of the surrounding training set.

To estimate these individual behaviors efficiently, the paper develops maximum-likelihood and amortized estimators that use a small number of noisy observations per point. These estimators support analysis of factors associated with different scaling patterns. The authors also demonstrate applications to data valuation and subset selection, connecting the observed laws to decisions about which examples to retain or prioritize.
icml-2024-scaling-laws-for-the-value-of-.tldr: Individual training examples follow different value-scaling patterns, making their relative usefulness depend on dataset size.

paragraphs: An observational dataset may not represent the population a decision maker cares about. Existing robust inference approaches can allow a specified amount of distribution shift, but that allowance may ignore useful knowledge about the target population. This paper develops a framework that incorporates such knowledge when drawing conclusions under selection bias.

The user supplies constraints as functions whose expected values are known in the target distribution. These constraints restrict the possible shifts between observed and target data. The method then returns high-probability bounds on the target quantity of interest. This is partial identification: the available evidence supports a range of values rather than necessarily determining one exact answer.

The authors analyze both the statistical and computational properties of estimating these bounds. They demonstrate informative results on simulated tasks, semisynthetic tasks, and a real-world use case. The approach matters because it turns domain knowledge into explicit restrictions on uncertainty, allowing conclusions to reflect what is known about the target population as well as what is observed in the dataset.
icml-2024-statistical-inference-under-co.tldr: Known expectations in a target population constrain selection bias and enable high-probability bounds on quantities of interest.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether generating time series in the frequency domain provides a useful advantage for diffusion models. Instead of representing a signal only through its values over time, the approach uses its Fourier representation. The question is whether that representation makes the structure of real time-series data easier for a generative model to learn.

Starting from the standard stochastic differential equation for time-domain diffusion, the authors derive a corresponding frequency-domain process. A key difference is that its noise involves mirrored Brownian motions, whose components have mirror symmetries. They use this result to adapt denoising score matching and construct frequency diffusion models with a formulation suited to that representation.

Experiments on real-world datasets, including healthcare and finance, show better capture of the training distribution than canonical time-domain diffusion models. The authors explain this through the greater localization of the studied signals in frequency space. The findings support frequency-domain representation as a useful modeling bias for these datasets, linking the empirical improvement to a structural property of the data.
icml-2024-time-series-diffusion-in-the-f.tldr: Frequency-domain diffusion better captures the studied time-series distributions, using a noise process that respects Fourier mirror symmetries.

paragraphs: Learning from human preferences requires feedback that can be expensive and difficult to collect across many topics. This paper explores automatically generated AI feedback as a scalable alternative. The authors identify both quantity and diversity as key factors, making broad coverage of user-assistant interactions part of the dataset’s design.

They expand the range and number of instructions and responses, then apply techniques intended to reduce annotation biases. The resulting UltraFeedback dataset contains more than one million pieces of GPT-4 feedback covering 250,000 user-assistant conversations and multiple assessment aspects. The contribution combines a large feedback resource with a process aimed at making that resource more varied and reliable.

Using UltraFeedback, the authors align a LLaMA-based model through best-of-n sampling and reinforcement learning. They report strong performance on chat benchmarks, supporting scaled AI feedback as a route to capable open-source chat models. The results connect the dataset-building choices to downstream model behavior and establish a resource for further research on learning from feedback.
icml-2024-ultrafeedback-boosting-languag.tldr: UltraFeedback supplies large-scale, diverse GPT-4 feedback and supports strong reported chat performance when used to align a LLaMA-based model.
